claim: The VPN FAQ says each Site-to-Site VPN connection has two tunnels and each tunnel supports a maximum throughput of up to 1.25 Gbps; for a connection to a virtual private gateway, aggregated throughput limits apply.
question: What is the approximate maximum throughput of a Site-to-Site VPN connection tunnel, according to the VPN FAQ?

values.spoken: one point two five gigabits per second

qualifiers.scope: per tunnel; a connection has two tunnels
qualifiers.condition: connection to a virtual private gateway: aggregated throughput limits apply

evidence.quote: Each AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection has two tunnels and each tunnel supports a maximum throughput of up to 1.25 Gbps. If your VPN connection is to a Virtual Private Gateway, aggregated throughput limits would apply.

note: FAQ question: 'What is the approximate maximum throughput of a Site-to-Site VPN connection?' (item 16). Large bandwidth tunnels (5 Gbps) are covered by facts from the user guide.

claim: Multiple VPN connections to the same virtual private gateway are bound by an aggregate throughput limit from AWS to on-premises of up to 1.25 Gbps; for Direct Connect on a virtual private gateway, the throughput is bound by the Direct Connect physical port.
question: Is there an aggregated throughput limit for a virtual private gateway with several VPN connections?

values.spoken: up to one point two five gigabits per second

qualifiers.scope: per virtual private gateway, all VPN connections together, AWS to on-premises
qualifiers.condition: VPN connections to a virtual private gateway

evidence.quote: Virtual Private Gateway has an aggregate throughput limit per connection type. Multiple VPN connections to the same Virtual Private Gateway are bound by an aggregate throughput limit from AWS to on-premises of up to 1.25 Gbps. For AWS Direct Connect connection on a Virtual Private Gateway, the throughput is bound by the Direct Connect physical port itself.

note: FAQ question: 'Is there an aggregated throughput limit for Virtual Private Gateway?' (item 17).

claim: To connect to multiple VPCs and achieve higher throughput limits than a virtual private gateway gives, the VPN FAQ says to use AWS Transit Gateway.
question: Which service does the VPN FAQ name for connecting multiple VPCs with higher VPN throughput limits?

values.spoken: use AWS Transit Gateway

evidence.quote: To connect to multiple VPCs and and achieve higher throughput limits, use AWS Transit Gateway.

note: FAQ question: 'Is there an aggregated throughput limit for Virtual Private Gateway?' (item 17). The page prints 'and and'.

claim: Each Site-to-Site VPN connection has two tunnels and each tunnel supports a maximum of up to 140,000 packets per second.
question: What is the approximate maximum packets per second of a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel, according to the VPN FAQ?

values.spoken: up to one hundred forty thousand packets per second

qualifiers.scope: per tunnel; a connection has two tunnels

evidence.quote: Each AWS Site-to-Site VPN connection has two tunnels and each tunnel supports a maximum packets per second of up to 140,000.

note: FAQ question: 'What is the approximate maximum packets per second of a Site-to-Site VPN connection?' (item 19).

claim: VPN connection throughput can depend on the customer gateway capability, the capacity of your connection, average packet size, the protocol, TCP versus UDP, and the network latency between the customer gateway and the virtual private gateway.
question: What factors affect the throughput of a Site-to-Site VPN connection?

values.display: the capability of your customer gateway
values.spoken: the capability of your customer gateway

evidence.quote: VPN connection throughput can depend on multiple factors, such as the capability of your customer gateway, the capacity of your connection, average packet size, the protocol being used, TCP vs. UDP, and the network latency between your customer gateway and the virtual private gateway.

note: FAQ question: 'What factors affect the throughput of my VPN connection?' (item 18).

claim: By default the customer gateway must initiate the IKE session; the AWS VPN endpoints can initiate it if you enable the appropriate options.
question: Which side of the VPN tunnel initiates the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) session by default?

values.display: your Customer Gateway (CGW) must initiate IKE
values.spoken: the customer gateway starts IKE

qualifiers.condition: the AWS VPN endpoints can initiate when the appropriate options are enabled

evidence.quote: By default your Customer Gateway (CGW) must initiate IKE. Alternatively, the AWS VPN endpoints can initiate by enabling the appropriate options.

note: FAQ question: 'Which side of the VPN tunnel initiates the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) session?' (item 30).

claim: When asked whether you can NAT your customer gateway behind a router or firewall, the VPN FAQ answers that you use the public IP address of your NAT device.
question: What address do you use when the customer gateway sits behind a NAT device?

values.display: the public IP address of your NAT device
values.spoken: the public IP of the NAT device

qualifiers.condition: customer gateway behind a router or firewall that does NAT

evidence.quote: You will use the public IP address of your NAT device.

note: FAQ questions: 'Can I NAT my customer gateway behind a router or firewall?' (item 22) and 'What IP address do I use for my customer gateway address?' (item 23) have the same answer.

claim: To avoid NAT-T you must disable it on your own device; if it stays enabled, AWS attempts to establish the tunnel over UDP port 4500, and if that port is not open the tunnel does not establish.
question: What happens if NAT-T is not disabled on the customer gateway device and UDP port 4500 is closed?

values.spoken: UDP port forty-five hundred

qualifiers.condition: NAT-T not disabled on the device and not planned to be used

evidence.quote: You will need to disable NAT-T on your device. If you don’t plan on using NAT-T and it is not disabled on your device, we will attempt to establish a tunnel over UDP port 4500. If that port is not open the tunnel will not establish.

note: FAQ question: 'How do I disable NAT-T on my connection?' (item 24).

claim: The AWS VPN service is route-based, so a route-based configuration meets no security association limits; a policy-based solution must limit itself to a single security association.
question: How many IPsec security associations can be established concurrently per tunnel, and what does that mean for policy-based devices?

values.spoken: a policy-based device is limited to one security association

evidence.quote: The AWS VPN service is a route-based solution, so when using a route-based configuration you will not run into SA limitations. If, however, you are using a policy-based solution you will need to limit to a single SA, as the service is a route-based solution.

note: FAQ question: 'How many IPsec security associations can be established concurrently per tunnel?' (item 25).

claim: A Site-to-Site VPN connection advertises a maximum of 1,000 routes to the customer gateway device.
question: What is the maximum number of routes that a VPN connection advertises to the customer gateway device?

values.spoken: up to one thousand routes

qualifiers.scope: per VPN connection, AWS to customer gateway device

evidence.quote: Your VPN connection will advertise a maximum of 1,000 routes to the customer gateway device.

note: FAQ question: 'What is the maximum number of routes that my VPN connection will advertise to my customer gateway device?' (item 27).

claim: You can advertise a maximum of 100 routes from the customer gateway device to a Site-to-Site VPN connection on a virtual private gateway, or a maximum of 1000 routes to a connection on an AWS Transit Gateway.
question: What is the maximum number of routes the customer gateway device can advertise to a Site-to-Site VPN connection?

values.spoken: up to one hundred routes on a virtual private gateway
up to one thousand routes on a transit gateway

qualifiers.scope: per VPN connection, customer gateway device to AWS; depends on the gateway type
qualifiers.condition: 100 for a virtual private gateway, 1000 for an AWS Transit Gateway

evidence.quote: You can advertise a maximum of 100 routes to your Site-to-Site VPN connection on a virtual private gateway from your customer gateway device or a maximum of 1000 routes to your Site-to-Site VPN connection on an AWS Transit Gateway.

note: FAQ question: 'What is the maximum number of routes that can be advertised to my VPN connection from my customer gateway device?' (item 28).

claim: For a VPN connection with BGP, the BGP session resets if the customer gateway attempts to advertise more than the maximum number of routes for the gateway type.
question: What happens to a BGP session of a VPN connection when the customer gateway advertises more routes than the maximum?

values.spoken: the BGP session resets

qualifiers.condition: more routes advertised than the maximum for the gateway type

evidence.quote: For a VPN connection with BGP, the BGP session will reset if you attempt to advertise more than the maximum for the gateway type.

note: FAQ question: item 28.

claim: For a VPN connection with static routes, you cannot add more than 100 static routes.
question: How many static routes can a Site-to-Site VPN connection with static routing have?

values.spoken: no more than one hundred static routes

qualifiers.scope: per VPN connection with static routes

evidence.quote: For a VPN connection with Static routes, you will not be able to add more than 100 static routes.

note: FAQ question: item 28.

claim: VPN connections to an AWS Transit Gateway can carry either IPv4 or IPv6 traffic, selected when you create the connection; the tunnel endpoint and customer gateway IP addresses are IPv4 only.
question: Do Site-to-Site VPN connections support IPv6 traffic, and which addresses stay IPv4?

values.spoken: tunnel endpoint and customer gateway addresses stay IPv4

qualifiers.scope: VPN connections to an AWS Transit Gateway
qualifiers.condition: select IPv6 with the tunnel option Inside IP Version

evidence.quote: VPN connections to an AWS Transit Gateway can support either IPv4 or IPv6 traffic which can be selected while creating a new VPN connection. To select IPv6 for VPN traffic, set the VPN tunnel option for Inside IP Version to IPv6. Note that tunnel endpoint and Customer Gateway IP addresses are IPv4 only.

note: FAQ question: 'Do VPN connections support IPv6 traffic?' (item 29).

claim: VPN connection-hours are billed for any time the VPN connection is in the available state; you terminate the VPN connection to avoid being billed for additional VPN connection-hours.
question: What defines billable VPN connection-hours?

values.spoken: while the connection is in the available state

evidence.quote: VPN connection-hours are billed for any time your VPN connections are in the "available" state. You can determine the state of a VPN connection via the AWS Management Console, CLI, or API. If you no longer wish to use your VPN connection, you simply terminate the VPN connection to avoid being billed for additional VPN connection-hours.

note: FAQ question: 'What defines billable VPN connection-hours?' (item 3). The VPC FAQ fact vpc-faq-vpn-connection-hour-billing also states per-hour billing.

claim: Private IP VPN connections need a transit gateway, and a private IP VPN attachment on the transit gateway requires a Direct Connect attachment for transport.
question: Do you require a transit gateway for Private IP VPN, and what transport does it need?

values.display: you need a Transit gateway to deploy private IP VPN connections
values.spoken: private IP VPN needs a transit gateway and a Direct Connect attachment

evidence.quote: Yes, you need a Transit gateway to deploy private IP VPN connections. Also, a private IP VPN attachment on Transit Gateway requires a Direct Connect attachment for transport.

note: FAQ question: 'Do I require a Transit gateway for Private IP VPN?' (item 33).

claim: The Private IP Site-to-Site VPN feature lets you deploy VPN connections to an AWS Transit Gateway using private IP addresses, and it works over an AWS Direct Connect transit virtual interface.
question: What does Private IP Site-to-Site VPN do, and over what does it work?

values.display: works over an AWS Direct Connect transit virtual interface
values.spoken: it runs over a Direct Connect transit virtual interface

evidence.quote: Private IP Site-to-Site VPN feature allows you to deploy VPN connections to an AWS Transit Gateway using private IP addresses. Private IP VPN works over an AWS Direct Connect transit virtual interface (VIF).

note: FAQ question: 'Do VPN connections support private IP addresses?' (item 31).

claim: AWS recommends BGP-capable devices when available, because BGP offers robust liveness detection checks that can assist failover to the second VPN tunnel if the first tunnel goes down.
question: Why does AWS recommend dynamic routing with BGP for a Site-to-Site VPN?

values.spoken: BGP detects a dead tunnel and helps fail over to the second one

evidence.quote: We recommend that you use BGP capable devices, when available, because the BGP protocol offers robust liveness detection checks that can assist failover to the second VPN tunnel if the first tunnel goes down.

note: FAQ question: 'Do private IP VPNs support static routing and BGP?' (item 34).

claim: Like regular Site-to-Site VPN connections, each private IP VPN connection supports 1.25Gbps and 5Gbps of bandwidth, and ECMP across multiple private IP VPN connections of both types increases effective bandwidth.
question: What throughput can you get with Private IP VPN?

evidence.quote: Just like regular Site-to-site VPN connections, each private IP VPN connection supports 1.25Gbps and 5Gbps of bandwidth. You can use ECMP (Equal Cost Multi-path) across multiple private IP VPN connections of both types to increase effective bandwidth.

note: FAQ question: 'What throughput can I get with Private IP VPN?' (item 36).

claim: Private IP VPN connections support 1500 bytes of MTU.
question: What is the MTU of a Private IP VPN?

values.spoken: fifteen hundred bytes

evidence.quote: Private IP VPN connections support 1500 bytes of MTU.

note: FAQ question: 'What is the MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) of Private IP VPN?' (item 38).
